desc:
A knight stands on cell (startRow, startCol) of an m x n board (0-indexed). A knight move changes the position by (+-2, +-1) or (+-1, +-2) and must stay on the board. A tour is a sequence of moves that starts on the given cell and visits every cell of the board exactly once; it does not have to return to the start.

Return the number of different tours. Two tours are different when they visit the cells in a different order.

For example, on a 3 x 4 board the knight has 2 tours from the cell (2, 0), on a 5 x 5 board it has 304 tours from the corner (0, 0), and on a 3 x 3 board it has none (the middle cell can never be visited).
hints: Count with backtracking: from the current cell try each of up to 8 knight moves to an unvisited cell, recurse, and add up the number of completed tours. A tour is complete when all m * n cells are used.
Keep the visited cells as a bitmask and precompute, for every cell, the list of cells a knight can jump to (and the same list as a bitmask).

Prune with dead ends: after a move, if an unvisited neighbour of the new cell has no unvisited neighbour of its own, it can only be the last cell of the tour, so if more than one cell is still unvisited, return 0 immediately.
editorial: A depth-first search with a visited bitmask enumerates every sequence of knight moves that never repeats a cell and counts those of full length. The branching factor of a knight is at most 8, but only about 2 to 3 moves are available on average, and there are strong constraints: corner cells have only two neighbours, so the tour must pass through them in a very specific way.

The dead-end rule makes the search practical for boards up to 25 cells: after stepping to a cell, look at the unvisited cells it attacks; one of them having no unvisited neighbour means it can be entered only from here and never left, so it must be the final cell. If there are still two or more cells to visit the whole branch is dead. The same test would also detect two such cells. With the rule, the worst start on a 5 x 5 board needs about 105 calls. Bit tricks keep the inner loop short: not (nbmask[v] & ~mask) means that v has no unvisited neighbour.
